groups.name: Parent & Me (2–3)
groups.intro: Every session here stands on its own, so families who join mid-year don't miss anything, while still following a monthly theme. The parent is the spotter and the main coach; you coach the parents.

w: Show your grown-up a new move

session.title: Warm-up, 10 min
session.detail: Free explore on mats, then a crawl-and-step path to the wall.

session.title: Station rotation, 20 min
session.detail: Four 5-minute stations families rotate through: the themed skill (coach shows parent, parent shows child), a free climb, a crawl or balance path, and a calm corner for anyone who needs a pause.

session.title: Water and song break, 5 min
session.detail: Sit together, drink water, a short movement song.

session.title: Story game, 15 min
session.detail: The week's story game, played in parallel by each family, restarting often with small changes.

session.title: Cool-down, 10 min
session.detail: Turtle landings, a goodbye song or cheer, tell parents one thing to try at the playground.

notes: No ropes, knots or belaying: feet stay within a short step of the mat.
Brave Steps replaces Hard Workout: one gentle stretch past last time, always the child's choice.

session.title: Warm-up, 10 min
session.detail: Story warm-up on the floor: animal walks, jumps, reaching for the sky.

session.title: Station rotation, 20 min
session.detail: Four 5-minute stations on low walls and mats: the skill of the week as guided play, a free climb, a floor balance or crawl game, and a coach-led "brave" climb.

session.title: Water break, 5 min
session.detail: Sit in a circle, drink water, retell the story so far.

session.title: Game, 15 min
session.detail: Game Day or the month's game, one rule only, adding a twist each round.

session.title: Cool-down, 10 min
session.detail: Falling Leaf landings and a closing cheer.

notes: Brave Climb Challenge replaces Hard Workout: each child picks one thing that felt scary or new and tries it once.
No races or "who went highest"; praise what they did with their feet and body.

weeks.skill: Review: Base Building & Systems (general prep) favorites

Arete: An outside corner edge of the wall.
The corner edge that sticks out.
Attempt: One go at a route; comps count them.
Back-Clip: Clipping a quickdraw so the rope runs from the wall side out toward the climber the wrong way, which can unclip in a fall.
Backstep: Standing on the outside edge with the hip turned in.
Standing on your pinky-toe side, hip turned to the wall.
Belay: Managing the rope to catch and lower a climber.
Holding the rope for your climber.
Belay Device: A device that adds friction so the belayer can hold and lower the climber.
The tool that helps the belayer hold the rope.
Belay Loop: The strong loop on a harness for the belay device.
The strongest loop on the front of your harness.
Beta: Information on how to do a route; unrequested beta is 'spray'.
The secret plan for a climb.
Body Tension: Engaging the core to keep feet on and body controlled.
Squeezing your middle so you stay stuck.
Brake Hand: The hand that never leaves the brake strand.
The hand that never lets go.
Breathing: Slow breathing to calm nerves and recover.
Bump: Moving one hand twice in a row to reach a better hold.
Carabiner: A metal clip with a gate; lockers have a sleeve that closes the gate.
A metal clip; lockers screw shut.
Center of Gravity: The body's balance point; climbers keep it over the feet.
Your body's balance spot, near your belly button.
Climbing Shoes: Snug, sticky rubber shoes for climbing.
Commitment: Fully attempting a move once you've decided it is a reasonable risk.
Going for the move all the way.
Crash Pad: Foam padding below boulders to reduce landing impact.
The squishy floor that cushions falls.
Crimp: A small, thin edge held with the fingertips; also the grip used on it.
A tiny ledge you hold with your fingertips.
Cross Through: Reaching one hand over or under the other.
Cut Feet: Feet coming off the wall, usually on steep terrain.
When your feet swing off the wall.
Deadpoint: A dynamic move catching a hold at the top of the body's movement.
A quick reach at the floaty moment.
Dihedral: An inside corner like an open book.
Downclimb: Climbing back down instead of dropping.
Drop Knee: Turning one knee down and in to bring the hip to the wall.
Twisting your knee down so your hip touches the wall.
Dynamic: Moving fast with a swing or jump.
Dyno: A jump where the body leaves contact to catch a hold.
Edging: Standing on a hold with the inside or outside edge of the shoe.
Standing on the side of your shoe.
Endurance: The ability to keep climbing a long time.
Climbing a long time without getting tired.
Fall Zone: The area under and around a climber where they might land; keep it clear.
The mat space where a climber could fall; stay out.
Falling!: Warning calls: 'Falling!' for the belayer, 'Rock!' for anything dropped.
Fear of Falling: Normal fear managed by gradual exposure and practiced falls.
Feeling scared to fall, which is normal.
Figure-8 Follow-Through: The standard tie-in knot; finish with a tail.
The knot that ties you to the rope.
Flagging: Placing a leg against the wall without a hold to balance.
Sticking a leg out like a tail to keep balance.
Foot Swap: Replacing one foot with the other on the same hold.
Foothold: A hold used for feet; small ones are called chips or jibs.
Frontstep: Standing on the inside edge, hips square to the wall.
Standing facing the wall on your big toe side.
Growth Mindset: The belief that ability grows with practice; coaches praise effort and strategy.
Your brain grows when you try hard.
Growth Plate: Growing bone ends in kids' fingers; hangboarding and full crimping are deferred for youth to manage injury risk.
The growing part of your finger bones that needs care.
Harness: Waist belt and leg loops that connect a climber to the rope.
The seat you wear to tie into the rope.
Heel Hook: Placing the heel on a hold and pulling with the hamstring.
Hooking your heel on a hold like a hand.
High Step: Placing a foot high, near the hip or hand.
A big step way up high.
Hold: Any shaped grip bolted to the wall for hands or feet.
The bumps on the wall you grab or stand on.
Isolation: Waiting area at comps where climbers can't see routes.
Jug: A large, deep, positive hold that is easy to grip.
A big hold shaped like a jug handle.
Knee Bar: Wedging the knee and foot between holds to rest.
Wedging your knee to rest your arms.
Landing Position: Landing on feet with bent knees, then rolling back, arms in.
Bend knees, land, roll back like a turtle.
Layback: Pulling on a side edge while pushing feet the opposite way.
Pulling and pushing opposite ways on an edge.
Lead Climbing: Climbing with the rope from below, clipping quickdraws on the way; falls are longer.
Bringing the rope up with you and clipping it as you go.
Lock-Off: Holding a bent arm still while the other hand reaches.
Freezing one arm bent while you reach.
Lower: Commands for coming down and ending the belay.
Coming down; feet out, sit back.
Mantle: Pressing down on a ledge to climb on top of it.
Pushing down like getting out of a pool.
Match: Putting both hands (or feet) on the same hold.
Observation Period: Comp time to read routes before climbing.
Time to look at the route at comps.
Onsight: Sending on the first try with no beta.
Overhang: Wall steeper than vertical; a roof is horizontal.
A wall that leans over you.
PBUS: A tube-device belay sequence: pull, brake, under, slide.
Partner Check: Checking each other's harness, knot, device and carabiner before every climb.
Checking your buddy's gear before climbing.
Pinch: A hold squeezed between thumb and fingers.
A hold you pinch like a crab claw.
Pocket: A hole in a hold for one or more fingers (one-finger pockets, monos, are not for youth).
A hole you poke fingers into.
Power Endurance: Repeating hard moves without much rest.
Doing hard moves again and again.
Project: A route worked over multiple sessions.
A hard climb you keep practicing.
Pump: When your arms feel tight and tired.
Quickdraw: Two carabiners joined by a sling, used to clip the rope to bolts when leading.
Two clips on a strap for lead climbing.
Quiet Feet: Placing feet without noise, which signals precision.
Putting your feet down so quietly nobody hears.
Rest: Time off the wall between attempts or sessions.
Resting so you can climb strong again.
Rest Position: A low-effort stance on the wall to recover, often with straight arms, shaking out each hand.
A comfy spot on the wall to rest your arms.
Rock Over: Shifting weight over a high foot to stand on it.
Moving your body over a high foot and standing up.
Rope: A stretchy dynamic rope that absorbs fall energy.
The stretchy rope that catches you.
Route: A designated path of holds, usually one color.
The holds you're allowed to use, all one color.
Route Reading: Planning a sequence from the ground.
Send: Completing a route from start to finish without falling.
Sidepull: A hold facing sideways, pulled toward the body's midline.
A hold you pull sideways, like opening a sliding door.
Slab: Wall less than vertical; balance and footwork terrain.
A wall that leans back toward you.
Sloper: A rounded hold with no edge; it relies on friction and body position.
A round, smooth hold you hug with your whole hand.
Smear: Pressing the sole flat on the wall with no foothold, using friction.
Pressing your shoe flat on the wall to stick.
Soft Catch: Letting a little rope give during a lead fall so the climber swings in gently.
Speed Climbing: Racing up a standardized route on auto belay or top rope.
Sportsmanship: Respecting others: taking turns, cheering, not spraying beta.
Being a good teammate and taking turns.
Spotting: Guiding a falling boulderer's hips and head toward the mat.
Helping a climber land on the mat.
Start Holds: The tagged holds a route starts on.
The hold with the tape where you start.
Static: Slow, controlled movement keeping three points on.
Moving slow and smooth like a sloth.
Stemming: Pushing feet and hands against opposing walls.
Pushing out on both sides of a corner.
Stopper Knot: A knot tied in the rope end so it can't pass through the device.
A knot at the rope end.
Straight Arms: Hanging on extended arms so the skeleton holds weight.
Hanging like a monkey with long arms.
Strength: Maximum force for single hard moves.
Tail: The extra rope past a knot.
The extra bit of rope left over.
Take: A call to pull rope tight and hold the climber.
Say 'take' to have your belayer hold you.
Three Points of Contact: Keeping three limbs on while one moves.
Tie-In Points: The two harness points the rope goes through to tie in.
The two loops your rope goes through.
Toe Hook: Hooking the top of the toes behind a hold.
Hooking the top of your toes on a hold.
Top Out: The finish of a problem: matching the last hold or climbing onto the top.
Top Rope: Climbing with the rope already running through an anchor above.
Climbing with the rope already at the top.
Training Log: A record of climbs, attempts and lessons.
Turning In: Rotating the hips so one side faces the wall, adding reach.
Twisting your hip to the wall to reach higher.
V-Scale: The bouldering difficulty scale, VB/V0 upward.
Numbers for how hard a boulder is.
Volume: A large hollow feature bolted to the wall, often with holds on it.
A giant shape on the wall you can stand or grab on.
Z-Clip: Clipping rope from below the previous draw into the next, creating a Z and heavy drag.
Grabbing rope from the wrong spot so it zigzags.
Zone: A mid-problem hold scoring partial points in comps.
